courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a Gaussian: position, covariance, opacity, SH color
md: Opacity is not the alpha used in blending. Alpha at a pixel is opacity times the Gaussian's falloff $G$ at that pixel, so the same Gaussian contributes strongly at its center and almost nothing a few standard deviations away.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: LL/SC detects *writes*, so it is immune to A to B to A in principle. In practice the pop needs a load between LL and SC, which hardware does not guarantee to support, and languages expose CAS anyway.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: If two stages interact, no single number per stage tells the whole story. Test the key combinations (a 2 x 2 grid for a suspected pair), and when you need a per-stage split of the total, use Shapley values, which sum exactly to the full-minus-baseline gain.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Client-side-only checks, tampering, and trusting what the client sends
md: Client input may say *what* is being requested. Only server-side state (the session, the database, the policy) may say *whether* it is allowed. If a value that decides access can be edited in the browser, the check is broken.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Privileged groups, and why so many paths lead to Domain Admins
md: Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins and built-in Administrators each control the domain (EA the whole forest). Nesting hides membership, and every machine an admin signs in to becomes a place to steal that admin. Keep these groups nearly empty and audit them recursively.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Forged tickets: golden and silver, and the double krbtgt reset
md: Golden tickets are forged TGTs from the krbtgt key; silver tickets are forged service tickets from one service key and never touch the KDC. Detect mismatches between tickets and the KDC's own logs, and evict with two krbtgt resets after closing the attacker's access.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Watching the domain, and recovering after it falls
md: Audit the DC events that reveal each attack and ship them off the DCs. After a domain compromise, contain first, then evict every credential (krbtgt twice), remove persistence, rebuild what you cannot trust, and keep offline AD backups.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: What this means for engineers: safe languages, fuzzing, defaults
md: Prevent, then detect, then mitigate. Memory-safe languages remove bug classes; sanitizers and fuzzing catch what remains; mitigations on by default raise the cost of what slips through; and fast patching shortens the window. Every rung an attacker must climb is one you can remove.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: The model does not execute tools. It only emits a structured request. Whether a shell command actually runs, and with what permissions, is decided entirely by harness code, which is why safety controls belong in the harness.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
md: The dangerous line is never the model call. It is the loop that turns model output into actions. Put your controls there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
md: Loading a pickle is running code. Prefer safetensors, load PyTorch files with weights_only=True, and verify a signature or hash from a source you trust before loading anything.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Green lists shift probabilities toward a keyed subset (distortionary). Gumbel sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact and hide the signal in correlations between chosen tokens and keyed random values. All of them need entropy to work.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: The fixed 0.5 cutoff of contamination="auto" is not calibrated to your data. In the 1000-point evaluation set of lesson 5 it flags 241 points when only 10 are anomalies. Rank by score, or set the threshold from a review budget, rather than trusting the default label.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: Misconception: "Only our app calls this API, so it is private." The app's traffic can be read and replayed by anyone who installs it, and API keys built into an app can be extracted from it. Treat every request as if a stranger typed it by hand.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Redirect URIs, the state parameter and OAuth CSRF
md: Misconception: state is optional decoration. Without state, PKCE, or nonce, any OAuth client can be logged into an attacker's account. RFC 6749 and RFC 9700 both make CSRF protection a must.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and the forged Microsoft tokens (2023)
md: A valid signature is only as good as the question "is this key one that this issuer uses for this kind of token?" RFC 8725 says it plainly: check that the keys belong to the issuer. And signing keys are crown jewels: rotate them, retire them, alert on their age, and log every use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secure code review: what a reviewer looks for
md: Review the flows, not the lines. For every value from outside, follow it to each sink and check the control at each trust boundary. Then ask the questions a tool cannot: should this exist, and who may use it?

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: CVE assignment and CNAs: who names a vulnerability
md: Fewer CVEs is not the same as fewer vulnerabilities. A vendor that fixes bugs silently looks clean while customers' scanners have nothing to match and never flag the old version. Judge vendors by how fast and how well they publish, not by the count.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: LSNs, pageLSN and the two tables recovery rebuilds
md: Do not mix up pageLSN and recLSN. In the example, P1 was first dirtied at LSN 10 and last changed at 60, so its recLSN is 10 while its pageLSN is 60. recLSN says where redo for the page might need to start; pageLSN says which changes the page already contains.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
md: Simplified: real embeddings are not interpretable feature lists, and the size of the effect varies by model and corpus. The toy shows the direction of the failure, not its typical magnitude. Lesson 5 is about measuring the magnitude on your data.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
md: Async does not make one request faster. It makes **waiting cheap**: a waiting connection costs a small saved object instead of a blocked OS thread with its own stack, so a few threads can serve many thousands of mostly idle connections.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS compares values, not history. If the value goes from A to B and back to A between your load and your CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless. For pointers in lock-free data structures (structures built from atomics instead of locks) it can be a real bug, the **ABA problem**, which has its own course later.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Who are you, prove it, and what may you do?
md: Identification is a claim, authentication is proof of the claim, authorization is permission. MFA means two different *kinds* of factor, not two secrets of the same kind.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
md: A session token is a password with an expiry date. Make it random (64+ bits), send it only as a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie, replace it at login, expire it on the server, and destroy it on the server at logout.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
md: More subagents is not automatically better. Anthropic's early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries and distracted each other with updates. Their prompts now embed effort rules: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3 to 10 tool calls, direct comparisons get 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each, and complex research uses more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Specific burndown rates, default quotas and tier prices change as models launch. Treat any number you remember as stale and read the current quota page and model card before you size a workload.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` (the standard Python model library) saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching (loading lines before the program asks for them, lesson 4) hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: XSS: when your page runs someone else's code
md: An `HttpOnly` session cookie does not make XSS harmless. It stops script from *reading* the cookie, so the attacker cannot take the session home. But the injected script does not need the cookie value: it sends requests from the victim's own browser, and the browser attaches the cookie for it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
md: Prevention lives in code (encode, sanitise, safe sinks, tokens, allowlists). Detection lives mostly in the browser (CSP and Trusted Types reports) and in monitoring of what your pages load. A team that only watches server logs is blind to DOM XSS and skimmers.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy
md: IAM starts from deny. A request is allowed only if some applicable policy explicitly allows it and no applicable policy explicitly denies it. Write policies as a list of what is needed, never as a list of what to forbid.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Catching misconfigurations early: infrastructure as code and CSPM
md: Scanners produce a lot of findings, and most teams drown in them. Rank by what an attacker could do: public exposure of sensitive data, wildcard IAM on roles reachable from the internet, IMDSv1 on internet-facing instances and disabled logging come before "detailed monitoring is off". A posture tool is only as good as the triage behind it.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: Arrow is not a file format for long-term storage like Parquet. Arrow data is laid out for fast random access and computation and is normally uncompressed in memory (the IPC format allows only optional LZ4 or ZSTD buffer compression); Parquet is encoded and compressed for small size on disk. A typical pipeline reads Parquet and decodes it into Arrow-style (or engine-specific) column vectors.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the screen continuously. It sees only the screenshots you return, at the moments you return them. If a dialog pops up after your capture, the model does not know about it until the next screenshot.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: Every source of non-determinism must come from loom: no real time, randomness or I/O inside `loom::model`. Determinism is what lets loom replay a schedule and flip one choice at a time.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it
md: Model A is **stronger** than model B when every history A allows is also allowed by B (A is a subset of B). Stronger models rule out more surprising results, and usually cost more coordination, latency or availability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
md: Consistent hashing balances keys. Hot keys need a different tool: copies (replication, client caches) for read-hot keys, splitting for write-hot keys, and miss coalescing for keys that expire under load.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
md: Choose the **variable** that is most likely to fail, and the **value** that is most likely to succeed. Every variable must be assigned eventually, so failing early on the hardest one costs nothing and prunes the most. But only one solution is needed, so values should keep the most options open.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
md: Misconception: "we scan, so our images are safe". A scanner only knows published vulnerabilities in recognised packages. It does not find your own code's bugs, a backdoored but unlisted dependency, or a secret left in a layer unless a secret scanner runs too.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
md: Misconception: "they can only create pods, not read Secrets". Pod creation lets them mount any Secret in the namespace into a pod they control and read it from inside. Treat create-pods as read-all-secrets for that namespace, unless admission policy restricts what pods may mount.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
md: Misconception: "our Secrets are encrypted because they look scrambled in kubectl". That is base64. Check whether the API server has --encryption-provider-config at all, and whether identity is first; the docs list both as signs that encryption at rest is not enabled.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
md: An image is an ordered list of content-addressed changesets plus a config. Everything else follows from that one sentence: identical layers are stored and transferred once, a deletion only adds a marker, and changing any layer invalidates every layer after it. Order your build steps from least to most frequently changing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: References point at a response, not at the conversation. Store the ordered ids you displayed, with a version, and resolve ordinals, attributes and *those* against that stored list.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
md: Misconception: "the monitor flags less often after training, so the model behaves better." A falling flag rate is what both genuine improvement and obfuscation look like. Without an independent ground-truth check of the behavior, you cannot tell them apart.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
md: A hash of a short or guessable value is not secret. There are only 10,000 four-digit PINs; hashing all of them takes a fraction of a second, so a stored SHA-256 of a PIN is as good as the PIN. Lesson 11 covers how passwords must be stored instead.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
md: If you ever write pow(m, e, n) in production code you have built textbook RSA. Call a library's OAEP or PSS function, or better, avoid RSA encryption entirely and use an elliptic-curve key exchange plus an AEAD.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
md: Encryption at rest did not save the secrets, because a running service must decrypt them to use them, and the attacker read the keys from a running process. The only secret a breached CI vendor cannot leak is one it never stored.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Turning on dual writes does not make the stores identical. It only covers objects written *after* the switch. Objects that are never updated again stay only in the old store until the backfill copies them.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: eBPF lets you run your own logic at the moment an event happens, inside the kernel, with a load-time proof that it cannot crash or hang the machine. bpftrace makes that a one-liner: probe, optional filter, action, and maps that summarize in the kernel.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Pruning does not automatically make a model smaller or faster. The LiteRT docs state that pruned models are the same size on disk and have the same latency; they only compress better. You get size savings from a sparse format or compression, and speed only from kernels or hardware that skip zeros. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once more than half the weights are zero.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: A small output-token cap is not a cheap way to get short reasoning. The model does not know about the cap, so it can be cut off mid-thought, and you pay for the thinking tokens with nothing to show. Use the effort or budget control that the model was trained to respond to.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
md: Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
md: General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE` software engineer, `SDET` software development engineer in test, `RN` registered nurse) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: A mitigation does not remove the bug. It removes one *route* from the bug to control. Patch the bug, prefer memory-safe languages for new code, and treat mitigations as the layer that protects you from the bugs you have not found yet.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: The unit of sharing between cores is the cache line, not the variable. Two variables in one line are shared as far as the hardware is concerned, whatever the source code says.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results
md: ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
md: Sampling cost is set by how curved the learned paths are. A perfectly straight, constant-speed flow is solved exactly by one Euler step.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: The scale is a full-precision real number kept outside the FP8 data (in FP32), not a change to the format's exponent bias. The FP8 paper chose this deliberately: a software scale can take any value, while a programmable bias could only shift by powers of two.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Group commit: one WAL flush makes many transactions durable
md: Group commit does not make any single commit faster. With one client there is nothing to share and latency is one full flush. It raises **throughput** when many sessions commit concurrently, and it keeps latency from exploding as they queue.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
md: A good campaign starts with small valid seeds per feature, a dictionary of the format's tokens, and a minimised corpus that you keep and reuse. When coverage plateaus, improve the inputs and harness rather than adding CPU time.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Variant analysis and patch diffing: one bug, many siblings
md: When you fix a bug, write its pattern down and search for it before closing the ticket. Shellshock needed six CVEs because the first fix addressed one symptom of a design problem; variant analysis and fuzzing the patched code found the rest.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
md: Both indexes trade exactness of the first step for speed: a trigram index proposes candidates by a cheap overlap count, a BK-tree rules out subtrees with the triangle inequality. Neither changes the final score; you still verify candidates with the metric you trust.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: Retrieval is cheap and noisy; verification is strict. Each match is a full alignment that predicts many other stars, and the Bayes factor multiplies independent evidence, so a true match passes 1e9 within a handful of stars while chance matches almost never do.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes
md: For a per-pixel operator, layout plus pitch decides how wide an aligned access each lane can make. NHWC gives a pixel's channels locality and lets one load carry a whole pixel when channels are padded to 4; NCHW gives each channel a unit-stride stream. Neither is wrong, and both lose if the kernel accesses one byte at a time.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Best fit plus split plus merge keeps reuse high, but a free hole only helps if it is big enough. Watch the gap between total free and the largest free block, not just the totals.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: Count distinct 32-byte sectors per warp request. 4 for 32 consecutive floats is ideal; 32 is the worst case and wastes 87.5% of the traffic.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Reading the Speed Of Light rows
md: Speed Of Light does not tell you what to fix. It tells you which of four investigations to open, and whether the kernel has any headroom at all.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
md: `__syncthreads()` may appear in conditional code only if the condition evaluates the same way for every thread in the block. Otherwise execution may hang or produce unintended side effects. Hoist the barrier out of the branch.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search never retrieves by similarity. It asks every community at one level, lets the LLM score how useful each partial answer is, and keeps the best points. That is what makes it work for questions that look like nothing in the corpus.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Group-relative advantages: the baseline from sibling answers
md: In GRPO a sample's advantage means "how much better than its siblings on the same question". If all siblings agree (all right or all wrong), there is nothing to learn from that question.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
md: A common bug is merging realtime messages instead of replacing state. With FULL_DATASET, a trip missing from the newest message must lose its prediction. Merging keeps stale predictions alive for trips that already finished or were dropped by the producer.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Out-of-order and speculative execution, from zero
md: Speculation is safe for *results* and unsafe for *secrets*. The CPU guarantees that mispredicted work never changes what a program computes, but it was never designed to hide that the work happened. Every attack in lessons 7 to 11 is a way to steer transient instructions and then read their footprint.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
md: A pool is memory you have given away. Those 3170 pages hold 6.2 GiB out of the page cache (the kernel's in-memory cache of file data) and away from every other process whether or not PostgreSQL is running. Over-sizing `nr_hugepages` is a common way to cause out-of-memory kills on a box that looks half empty.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
md: Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
md: Averaging fixes errors that differ from sample to sample. It cannot fix an error every sample shares, such as the LLM misunderstanding an ambiguous or unfamiliar query. That is the root of HyDE's main failure mode in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
md: Secure protocols only help when they are on. An OPC UA server left in mode None, a DNP3 outstation without SAv5 keys, or a Modbus/TCP Security device that also listens on plain port 502 gives the attacker the old, unauthenticated path.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
md: Two IT reflexes can hurt in OT: rebooting or reimaging a running HMI or server (NIST: rebooting 'may not be acceptable'), and running active scans across the control network during an incident. Both can stop the process or the operators' only view of it.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
md: RFC 3227 names programs to avoid on a live suspect system, such as `tar` or `xcopy`, because they update the access time of every file they touch, overwriting evidence of what the attacker read.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
md: Clocks start at awareness or determination, not at the end of the investigation. If you wait until you know everything, you will be late. Plan for phased notices: first what you know, then updates.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
md: Patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. After an injection that may have been exploited, look for persistence (web shells, new accounts, changed configuration) and for what data left, using web, database and network logs.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
md: Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: Three defences, in order: prune what cannot run, search within a budget you chose from a convergence curve, and promote only wins that are larger than the noise. A tuner without the third one is a random walk through your performance history.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: For memory-bound kernels, runtime is roughly bytes moved / bandwidth. Elementwise ops do so little math per byte that the only lever that matters is how many bytes cross the HBM boundary. Fusion cuts bytes, not FLOPs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
md: Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Keys: quantize per channel, because outliers live in fixed channels. Values: quantize per token, because the output mixes value rows. Keep the most recent tokens in full precision until a group is complete.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Offloading does not make attention read from CPU memory. In reuse offloading, blocks are copied back into GPU blocks before the attention kernel runs; the kernel only ever sees HBM. What offloading buys is skipping the *prefill compute* that would otherwise recreate those blocks.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: Happened-before means *information could have flowed* from a to b through process order and messages. It is a partial order: many pairs of events are simply concurrent, and no clock reading can change that.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: MaxSim: each query token finds its best document token
md: Why max and not average? The ColBERT ablation (an experiment that swaps out one component, retrains, and measures what changes) replaced max with average similarity and MRR@10 dropped noticeably. In the toy, the *founded* row of Doc A averages (0.03 + 0.02 + 0.18 + 0.98 + 0.49) / 5 = 0.34, even though the document contains a near-perfect match. Averaging punishes documents for having other content.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: n continuous thoughts cost n sequential forward passes at inference and n + 1 sequential passes per training example, with no tokens emitted for the latent steps.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: An RMI separates model size from execution cost. A lookup evaluates exactly one model per stage, however many leaf models exist. Adding leaves makes each leaf's slice smaller and its error bounds tighter without adding work per lookup.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
md: Setting a user's shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin` or putting `*` in their password field does not fully disable them. The passwd manual notes such users may still run jobs through cron or log in by other means, and an SSH key in their home directory still works if the shell allows it. To retire an account, lock it, expire it and remove its keys.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Keys beat passwords because nothing guessable or reusable travels to the server. That moves the risk to the key files themselves: `authorized_keys` decides who gets in, so audit it like you audit sudoers.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
md: Label-level agreement can be modest (kappa 0.3 to 0.6) while system-level agreement is high (tau near 0.9), because errors that are not systematic average out over many queries. The reverse also holds: a small systematic bias can flip close systems even when kappa looks fine.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
md: Report a gain as an interval, computed by resampling items with both systems paired. If the interval includes zero, say "not distinguishable on this set" and either add items or keep the old version. Check slices as well as the average.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
md: Three different promises are easy to confuse: *parses as JSON*, *matches my schema*, and *is correct*. JSON mode gives the first, schema-constrained output gives the second, and only your own validation and evaluation can check the third.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: The predictions in this lesson are hand-written to show typical error types. They are not measurements of any model. Use the method, not the numbers.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
md: Every input saving has a quality price. Truncation can cut the sentence that made a passage relevant. A smaller $k$ means relevant documents retrieved at rank 31 or lower are never reranked. Measure NDCG@10 at each setting on your own queries before shipping the cheaper one.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT
md: Read router claims carefully. "2x cheaper at the same quality" depends on the benchmark, the model pair, the quality target and the baseline. RouteLLM's savings are measured against a random router, not against a GPT-4-only deployment, and vary from 1.41x to 3.66x across three benchmarks. Only an evaluation on your own prompts tells you what you will get.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: RANSAC finds the model that the most matches agree on by fitting minimal random samples. The cost grows as $1/w^s$, so cleaner matches (a good ratio test) and smaller samples make it dramatically cheaper.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell
md: Vyukov is explicit: the queue is "not lockfree in the official meaning, just implemented by means of atomic RMW operations w/o mutexes" (RMW is read-modify-write: an instruction such as CAS or fetch-add that reads and writes a location in one indivisible step) and classifies it as having blocking producers and consumers. It is still excellent in practice; just do not cite it as a lock-free progress guarantee.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The misconception that costs the most: that a template id is a stable name for a logging statement. It is a name for a *cluster*, and clusters split, merge, get wildcarded and get evicted. Anything long-lived (a dashboard, an alert rule, a trained model) must key on persisted template text plus an explicit supersedes relation, not on whatever integer the miner handed out last Tuesday.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
md: A green cell is not protection. One rule tagged with a technique usually catches one or two of the many ways to perform it. Count a technique as covered only if a test of a realistic procedure produced an alert (lesson 17), and record which procedures were tested.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank (the rank of a matrix is how many independent directions its outputs can point in), so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
md: Every behaviour rule has false positives: per-user installers for chat and sync clients legitimately write Run keys from AppData. Sigma's falsepositives field is not decoration; tune with an allowlist of known-good signed programs and review what fires.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: "Fragmentation is solved" is not the lesson. The study covers eight single-threaded C and C++ programs from the 1990s, and the authors call for more work on unusual program behaviour. Long-running servers with phase changes, many threads and per-thread caches are exactly that kind of workload, as the next lesson shows.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: `volatile` is not an ordering. In standard C++, volatile accesses are not atomic and do not order other memory, so they cannot be used for synchronization between threads. (MSVC, Microsoft's C++ compiler, gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads (more runnable threads than cores, so some are always preempted), update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
md: Every allocation size and every length passed to memcpy should come from a computation that cannot overflow and a value that cannot be negative. When a size comes from a file or a packet, validate it against the real data first.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS (a video-based re-ID dataset) in their supplementary material.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Repeat, interleave, and report the mean with a confidence interval (or a median with its spread). Never decide from one run or from the best of N.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: Union and RRF are not interchangeable. A union returns everything (N x k documents at worst) in retrieval order, so taking its first k usually just returns the first query's list. Pick RRF when the next stage has a fixed budget; pick union when a reranker will score all candidates anyway.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
md: **Distillation** turns an expensive stage into a teacher for a cheaper one. Run the slow model offline on training queries, then train a fast model to imitate its rankings. You pay the teacher's cost once, at training time, instead of on every query.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
md: Shampoo and SOAP are often called *second-order*, but they do not compute the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives of the loss that true second-order methods such as Newton's method use. Like AdaGrad and Adam, they build preconditioners from products of gradients ($GG^\top$ and $G^\top G$).

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muP is not a formula that predicts the best SP learning rate for a bigger model. It changes how every layer's init and update scale with width, so a wide muP model trains differently from (and in the paper's experiments, better than) a wide SP model.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
md: `spin_loop()` is not `yield` (such as Rust's `std::thread::yield_now()`, which asks the operating system scheduler to run another thread for now). It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version
md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
md: Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: NeMo RL separates *what the algorithm does* (a single-controller loop written as if on one GPU) from *where it runs* (RayVirtualCluster plus RayWorkerGroups). Swapping vLLM for another engine, or changing GPU counts, should not change the algorithm code.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: BGP hijacks and route leaks: the MyEtherWallet case
md: A BGP hijack does not need to touch your servers or your users' networks. It moves traffic somewhere else on the internet, where your TLS certificate, DNSSEC signatures and user training are the remaining defences.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
md: Every packet is a header plus a payload. Every device on the path must read the header to deliver it, and can read the payload too unless it is encrypted. Both facts drive almost everything in network security.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
md: TLS protects the content of one connection between two endpoints. It does not hide who talks to whom, it does not make the server trustworthy, and it does not protect data once it is decrypted at either end.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
md: User programs run in ring 3 and can only ask; the kernel runs in ring 0 and decides. A system call is the only door between them. Sandboxing is mostly the art of closing doors and narrowing what each open door accepts.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS
md: A broker is only as good as its request checking. A broker that performs "open this path" for any path a renderer names has turned itself into a tool for the attacker. That failure has a name, the confused deputy, and it is the subject of lesson 15.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
md: Cubins run only on the same major CC with an equal or higher minor; PTX JIT compiles forward to any equal or higher CC. Ship cubins for the GPUs you target plus PTX for the newest one, and keep the list short for development builds, because every entry multiplies CUDA compile time.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Flaky means uncontrolled state. Reproduce with the exact node id, order seed and loop count, find the state, and control it with a fixture. Reruns and quarantine are temporary and cost real signal.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: Whatever the tool, the author's loop is the same: answer every comment, change the code where the reviewer was right, record what changed between versions, and carry earned review credit forward only while it still applies.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Misconception: "syncing my fork" updates my laptop. GitHub's Sync fork button updates the fork on GitHub; `git fetch upstream` plus a merge updates your local copy. GitHub's docs point out that syncing locally does not update the fork on GitHub until you push. They are separate repositories.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: Misconception: `-s` signs the commit. It does not. `-s` (lowercase) adds a Signed-off-by text trailer, a legal statement. `-S` (uppercase, `--gpg-sign`) adds a cryptographic signature made with your private key, by default through GPG (GNU Privacy Guard), that GitHub can show as Verified. A project may require either, both, or neither.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: Outbound is what users get; inbound is what the project gets from you. Inbound=outbound needs no paperwork; a CLA is a one-time signed grant, often with an explicit patent license and a statement about your employer.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Reporting honestly: geomeans, many benchmarks and costs
md: Do not cherry-pick. Quoting only the best benchmark, dropping a regressed one, or rerunning until a borderline result flips are all ways to make noise look like a win. Reviewers who rerun your commands will find out.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A screenshot of a traceback is not complete. The maintainer cannot search it, copy the line numbers, or paste it into a test. Stack Overflow's guide says plainly: do not use images of code; paste text.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: The right size for a PR is **one self-contained change**: it does one thing, includes its tests, and leaves the system working. Line counts are a symptom; focus is the goal.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
md: Knowing the exact output length would not fix this. Orca (Oracle) assumes perfect knowledge and still stores real token states in only 38.2% of KV memory, because contiguous chunks of different sizes still fragment the space and still cannot be shared.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: What a penetration test is, and what it is not
md: A scan asks *what might be wrong*. A pentest asks *what can an attacker actually do here, inside this scope*. A red team asks *would we notice and stop them*. A bug bounty asks the crowd, continuously, within published rules.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Attack surface management: recon as a defender
md: Attackers run recon against you continuously and for free. Run it yourself first: inventory what is exposed, diff it on a schedule, and treat every unexpected change as an incident until explained.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: Comparing two flame graphs by eye is error-prone because widths are relative to each graph's own total. To check a fix, record both under the same load and diff the folded files (a differential flame graph), and make sure you have enough samples for the change to stand out from noise.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: Common misconception: "only careless people fall for phishing". The UK NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) notes that people click for many reasons, including situational ones such as being busy and stressed, and that blaming them does not work. Blame also stops people reporting mistakes, which is the signal defenders need most.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Business email compromise and invoice fraud
md: BEC defeats technical email security by design: the best version comes from a real, authenticated account. The control that stops it is a payment process that does not trust email for changes to where money goes.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields
md: Bottom-up is not free of crowd effects. The CNN pass is constant, but the number of candidate pairs per limb grows with the number of people, and the whole image goes through the network at one input size, so small, distant people cover only a few heatmap pixels, while top-down resizes every person to the same crop size.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Query planners: choosing a strategy by selectivity
md: No single plan wins everywhere. Broad filters favor graph search with the filter applied during or after it; restrictive filters favor brute force over an allow list; the middle is where graphs fragment and filter-aware indexes like ACORN and Filtered-DiskANN earn their keep. The deciding input is the estimated number of matches.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 2: jobs, scripts and paths that root trusts
md: The same rule covers the files that define privilege themselves. A writable `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers.d/` entry or systemd unit directory is instant root. Treat any group or world write bit under `/etc` or `/usr` as a finding.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
md: Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: The one number to remember is not the microseconds of a single switch but **switches per second times total cost per switch**, where total includes the cache and TLB refill. Keep CPU-bound threads near the core count, and reserve extra threads or async I/O for work that actually waits.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
md: The data that chose the prompt cannot also grade it. Report the selected prompt's score on a held-out set that played no part in any choice, and expect it to be lower than the dev score.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Do not "fix" decode errors with `errors="ignore"` in security tooling. It silently deletes the bad bytes, so `ad\xffmin` becomes `admin` and your report shows a username the attacker never sent. Prefer `replace`, which leaves a visible mark.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Never decode and then *run* what you decoded to see what it does. Decode to text, read it, and search it. Executing an unknown PowerShell or shell command, even in your own terminal, is how an analyst becomes the next victim. Use an isolated analysis sandbox if you truly need behaviour.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
md: Feedback is only as good as its top k. When the first-pass top results are relevant, PRF finds words the user never typed; when they are off-topic, it amplifies the error. On MS MARCO dev, the query2doc paper reports BM25 MRR@10 18.4 against 15.8 for BM25 + RM3, while recall@1k rose slightly (85.7 to 86.4).

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
md: A Raft leader commits by counting replicas **only** for entries from its own current term. Older entries become committed indirectly, when a later current-term entry after them commits. Entries keep their original term number forever, which is why this rule is needed.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
md: Per-field BM25 features are not BM25F. BM25F (the subject of Elasticsearch's `combined_fields` query) merges term frequencies across fields before saturating. Separate per-field features saturate each field on its own and let the model weigh them. Both are useful; they are different numbers.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
md: Disagreement between metrics is information, not noise. If binary metrics and exponential nDCG disagree, your system is trading coverage of relevant documents against putting the very best one first. Report at least one metric of each kind and say which user you care about.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: In practice: register big pools on huge pages, keep the number of connected QPs bounded (share, or use UD for fan-out), batch posts behind one doorbell, inline small payloads, signal selectively, avoid hot atomics, and handle error completions by resetting or recreating the connection.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (mean absolute error, the average size of the gap between predicted and true rating) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: Misconception: reward hacking means the RL algorithm is buggy. DeepMind's analysis points the other way: the behavior comes from misspecification, and a *better* optimizer is more likely to find an intricate loophole that a weaker one would miss. Stronger RL makes the specification matter more, not less.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: Governance decides who decides. Risk management decides what is worth doing. Compliance proves to outsiders that you did what you are obliged to do. They overlap, but a company can be compliant and still badly governed, or well governed and still breached.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
md: Gordon-Loeb's lessons for engineers: spend where a dollar reduces the most expected loss, not where the scariest weakness is; for the paper's broad families of breach functions the optimum is at most about 37 percent of expected loss; and making controls more effective beats making budgets bigger.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: One control, many frameworks: CIS Controls, HIPAA and the crosswalk
md: Do not run one programme per framework. Write each control once, build it to the strictest applicable requirement, map it to every framework it satisfies, and attach evidence that is collected automatically. Start from CIS IG1 if you have nothing; use the crosswalk to answer everyone else.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Insurance does not replace controls or accountability. Regulators still fine you, customers still leave, and a claim can fail if your application overstated your controls or the event falls under an exclusion. Treat the policy wording as a contract engineers should read: what counts as a covered event, which notice deadlines apply, which incident responders you must use.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: Weighted fairness in sched_ext can be three lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Everything else (CPU placement, preemption, latency boosts) is extra policy you choose to add.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Brewer-Nash's Chinese Wall, and choosing the right model
md: A formal model is a precise statement of what secure means for one kind of system. Pick the model by the harm you fear: disclosure, contamination, invalid change, or conflict of interest. Real systems combine several.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Segmentation and microsegmentation, planned from real traffic
md: Segmenting by host pairs is not the finish line. The billing app still talks to the domain controller; restrict that flow to the authentication ports it needs and to the app's own identity, and watch it closely.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
md: Ask "who would want this asset, and what would they do with it?" Criminals want quick money and reuse easy entry points such as stolen passwords. States want long, quiet access.
